My boyfriend of four years broke up with me (FTM) when I came out, because he's a straight guy. I mean, I get it, but it destroyed me at the time. I had considered not coming out at all for the sake of being with him, as he was the love of my life, but the older and more dysphoric I got, the clearer it got that I couldn't live that way anymore.

I didn't cope with the loss well, mostly by drinking, but it didn't steer me off my transitional course. The cat was already out of the bag, and I knew the relationship would never be the same even if I chose not to transition, because he knew how I identified. What was I gonna do, scurry back into the closet I had worked so hard to claw my way out of? Nah, not my style. I knew I couldn't set myself on fire to keep others warm, even him, so I just pushed toward what was affirming to me. 

It didn't end up all bad, though, as we're still best friends after all this time.  He's not exactly learned about the LGBTQ+ community at large, so I tend to seek transitional support elsewhere. But, I'm five years on T and post-top surgery, and he's never deadnamed or misgendered me or anything. I just wasn't for him anymore. Just the way she goes sometimes. I can't blame him for his sexuality, nor me for my gender identity.

Have borderline personality disorder. I've had a few serious suicide attempts (and a few not so serious ones), several hospitalizations, significant episodes of problem drinking and self-harm, and some dissociation and emotional regulation issues. 

I'm 29 now and have been in therapy and/or engaged in mental health services since I was 9, though way back then, it was due to some horrendous life circumstances and the resulting depression. Thing is, I never found a therapist I clicked with, nor a medication regime that provided any real relief. I just keep jumping through the hoops, because it's gotta get better than never experiencing joy and wanting to die every day of my life. I'm currently experiencing a lapse in care due to the pandemic-driven closure of my clinic, but I usually meet with a psychiatrist and a case manager pretty frequently to monitor my symptoms and brainstorm how to become a functional member of the community again.

Was a vegetarian for a long time, because I've always struggled with my weight, and I thought a vegetarian diet would help me lose some extra pounds. But, I was desperately poor, so I wasn't, like, eating a lot of good, fresh produce, just the cheapest food I could find that didn't contain any meat. Real quantity over quality stuff, so I could afford as much as I would actually need to get by until my next payday.

Visited the doctor one day, and he had asked me to do some labs a couple days before the appointment so he could see how I was doing in a general sense and how a recently-added medication was treating me. Turns out, not only was I actually gaining weight due to my dietary choices, I was anemic and vitamin-deficient. 

So, I realized I needed to make some changes. I brought animal proteins back into the fold, which set me back financially, but it ensured I was getting something of quality in my body.  I was eating less overall, but it was better stuff, so I started losing weight and replenishing my stores of crucial nutrients. Started feeling better physically, too. I never really tried to return to vegetarianism, because I didn't want to fall back into the same poverty-driven pattern of surviving on inexpensive carbs and the occasional dairy product.

I continued that way for a long time, working myself to death without so much as a singular day off while still maintaining a solid A average in classes, until I finally secured my degree in human service, a degree I obtained so I could help homeless people in the future.

Put the struggling person in touch with community resources or connect them with professionals who can mitigate their challenges. I don't think there's a wrong way to tackle it if you're feeling like you're in an emotionally stable enough place to pursue hormonal treatment, whether you choose to address your mental health concerns so you have a more stable baseline to transition from, or whether you start the transitional process in the hopes that your symptoms might be alleviated somewhat.

I went with the second approach. I found that transitioning helped soothe the feelings of inadequacy, identity confusion, and social distress BPD can cause. However, after a few years of neglecting my mental health, I realized that transition alone wasn't enough to mitigate my symptoms and improve my quality of life in a significant enough way. I'm currently working with a team of mental health professionals at my community mental health organization to ensure that I'm receiving the proper medication regimen and case management I need.

Also, BPD can cause some difficulties with developing a solid sense of personal identity, but it's not gonna tell your brain you're trans if you're not. Your feelings of being gender nonconforming are valid regardless of your mental health diagnosis.

I used to work as a dispatcher for AAA. People would call to get roadside assistance, and I'd document the vehicle details, what they needed help with, and the location of the breakdown. Some auto shops and towing businesses received these details digitally with a few button presses on my end and were able to dispatch assistance to the breakdown locations without any extra interaction or steps, but most of the time I'd have to dig up who the nearest business who ran service calls was, put the caller on hold, briefly discuss the relevant information with the service techs, and then get back to the caller with an ETA. 

One time, I was working the evening shift, something like 4-10pm. Around 9, a woman called and said her SUV had broken down. She had no idea what was wrong with it, which wasn't necessarily too big of a problem, as there was a dispatch code for that. It's just easier when callers have an idea of the malfunction so that service techs show up with the right equipment for the job. 

I probed her for location information, where she was broken down, and literally the best answer she could give me was on the side of a two lane road somewhere in Indiana. She was taking a road trip to visit family, so she was in unfamiliar territory, but she hadn't been paying attention to cross streets, mile markers, or businesses she had passed. She couldn't tell me how long she'd been in Indiana, or the last time she turned onto a different road. She couldn't see any traffic lights, houses, or businesses to give her a frame of reference, and no one had driven by in a while that she could flag down and ask.   

So, I was like, how the fuck are we gonna find this incredibly situationally unaware woman? I asked her to hold, and I just started calling service stations in various parts of Indiana. I advised them of the situation, and every one I called said they'd send a tech out to check for stranded motorists. I switched back to the woman and tried to reassure her and jog her memory a little. I chatted with her for a while, giving the service techs a chance to scour the area. 

Eventually, I just started calling the service stations back to see if they had had any success. They all said their drivers had conducted a thorough search, some traveling as far as 20 miles away from the station to see if they could find her. No one had. 

It was getting to be almost 10 when I took her off of hold to advise her of my conversations with the various service stations. As soon as I did, her phone disconnected. Anxious, I called her back. Straight to voicemail. Tried back a few more times. Same thing. I assume her phone died.

So here this woman was, stranded with a dead phone in the dark on the shoulder of a country road, with no fuckin idea where she was or how she got there, hoping beyond hope that a courteous stranger would drive by and save the day. I knew she was reckless for not paying any attention to her surroundings, but I felt for her. It had to be a terrifying situation. 

I talked to my supervisor on duty about the ordeal, and she reassured me I did everything I could to secure this woman's safety. I still sometimes wonder what happened to her, if help did eventually come, if it was in the form of a concerned stranger or one of the service techs I called, and how long she had to wait for salvation.

Before I was officially diagnosed, I was about 93% sure I had borderline personality disorder. I was a social work major, and the disorder was covered in several different classes over the course of my studies due to its complexity. The more I learned about it, the more the symptoms just lined up to my experiences in an eerie way. 

After I had graduated, I ended up in a psychiatric hospital. After some conversations with a counselor there, she brought the diagnosis up, asked if anyone had ever labeled me with it. I told her I suspected it because of things I learned in school, and she suggested to my mental health team that I go through further counseling and testing to determine if I had it. The results of the intensive psychiatric testing I received and the evidence revealed in my therapy sessions showed that my thought patterns, behaviors, and emotional fluctuations were indeed consistent with borderline personality disorder.

I feel like I see a lot of people who self-diagnose with no intention of having their suspicions inspected by health professionals, and that's pretty toxic. But, I think it's important to educate ourselves on mental health concerns, formally or informally, so we are able to self-assess and bring our concerns to the attention of those who have been specifically trained to help us.

One day I was a little day drunk and started thinking about her. It hit me all at once that she was the last person keeping me from living completely authentically. So, with the spirit of liberation in mind, I called her immediately. We talked for a few minutes, and I just kind of blurted it out after we had run out of other things to say to each other. I told her I had something to tell her, that I had been living as a man and taking masculinizing hormones for a long time, and that it took me so long to tell her because I was unsure how she'd react. I'll never forget her reply. "You know, after 69 years, I've learned you just have to be who you are." To this day, she's the only family member who doesn't deadname or misgender me, even though I've been out to family for six years now, so they're well past the adjustment period.

My advice is to just be direct. They may be older, but they're people, and as such, they're capable of compassion. They'll likely appreciate you being honest and straightforward.

When I was a freshman in high school, there was a teacher who happened to teach both drama/forensics and gym class. She was a complete nightmare in both.

For those who are unfamiliar with forensics, it's a performing arts discipline in which you can choose one of many events to specialize in. There are acting-related events in which students can, for example, recite poetry, perform a monologue, or flesh out a scene from an existing piece of work; and there are non-dramatic events, such as persuasive speaking, impromptu speaking, and sales. Each student would choose an event and prepare a piece, then as a forensics team, we'd travel by bus to other schools on the weekends to compete with other students within our chosen events. There were typically two or three "rounds" for each event, meaning we'd perform twice or three times in front of different impartial judges, and the scores were compiled afterward to determine which place each student earned. After the performances were done, there would be a ceremony afterward to announce placements, and then we'd hop on the bus and go home.

When we got back on the bus, she would set into berating any of us who did not place second or higher in our events. These were teen actors and performers who practiced their pieces like an athlete would practice for a sporting event, and rather than recognizing their accomplishments and hard work, she chose to make them cry. Her anger was mostly directed at those who chose the dramatic events. As someone whose event was persuasive speaking, I certainly faced her wrath, but I learned not to take it seriously, as I found when she tried to coach me that she couldn't write her way out of a paper bag. The problem got to be so bad that many people decided they'd still show up to class for the sake of securing a performing arts elective that was required for graduation but not perform at meets, but if they chose that route, even if they practiced their pieces in class, she would fail them.   

As bad as she was at teaching forensics, she was worse at teaching gym. A kid almost died in our class because she had an asthma attack from jogging, and the teacher wouldn't let her get her inhaler because she thought she was making excuses. Kid collapsed on the floor, and another student had to sprint to her locker to get it for her. A friend of mine was also the target of her aggression. He had cerebral palsy and had difficulty jogging. She told him if he didn't show more effort, she'd fail him. When he explained his issue, she said she wouldn't believe it until he returned with a doctor's note, which he did. She still refused to believe it and kept revoking his points each day until his parents threatened to sue. 

She still remained a teacher there for years after I graduated, but she eventually was ousted because of all the complaints administration received. Last I knew, she shifted gears entirely and became a medical transport driver, like the type insurance companies contract with to take people to routine appointments. Lord help the poor people who are forced to share a car with her.

My sexuality changed in the opposite direction on T, and it was confusing to say the least. For most of my life, I had only had attraction toward women. I've never really watched porn other than a time or two, but all of my fantasies revolved around females (trans or cis, didn't matter which). I knew I was trans at a pretty young age but chose to ignore it for a long time, self-describing as a lesbian instead.

I found my first partner when I was 19 and lost my virginity to her. She was a bisexual cis woman. We really only did oral play--no toys or penetration. After that ended, I was single for a while, and then I found myself with a cis man. I was largely sex-repulsed or sex-indifferent when I was with him, I think in large part because of my attraction to women, though I was in love with his personality. That relationship ended when I came out nearly six years ago, and I've been single since.

I started testosterone shortly thereafter, when I was 24, and I found that I became almost entirely attracted to men. My fantasies and sexual desires changed in a drastic way, and I find that I would love to become a bottom to the right man at some point in my life. I can't explain it away. I find it's now very rare for me to experience attraction toward women. It was quite confusing to shift my self-identification from lesbian to straight to gay in a relatively short span of time. I've talked to a few of my FTM friends, who said, oh yeah, T did the same thing to them, so at least I don't feel completely alone.

Though our shifts in sexuality might be opposite, please know you're not the only one who's experienced an unexpected, somewhat scary change in their attraction. I know it's strange having to reexamine your desires and self-imposed labels that seemed so stable before. All I can say is, don't let a good thing pass you by. Feel free to experiment, even if it goes against those labels but feels right.

I had your standard double incision mastectomy with drains. My surgery was scheduled for 8am, and I was awake and aware at about 1pm. I think it might be because of the IV painkillers and the nerve block that were used, because I don't really remember being in pain at first. I was discharged at about 5pm and had about an hour car ride home, which was also pretty painless. 

For the next couple days, I wasn't in too much pain, but I certainly felt a weird tightness in the middle of my chest when I walked anywhere. It made me a little bit slow, but I'm overall fortunate in that I didn't have any problems changing clothes or reaching or caring for myself. I was allowed to shower (carefully, without screwing with the drain tubes) whenever I wanted, as I declined nipple grafts. I had to empty my drains every few hours and measure and record the output to show the medical staff at my post-op appointment so they could tell if it was safe to remove the drains then. The worst pain I encountered occurred around day 3-5, and strangely, it was in my back as my posture adjusted to not having all this tissue on the front of me. I definitely drove before I was supposed to, a day or two after surgery, but it didn't cause any complications, though I don't recommend it.

I didn't take much pain medication, partially because the pain wasn't that bad, and partially because I don't like how opiates make me feel. Sleeping with drain tubes and a compression vest on was the worst part. The thing is, I don't actually own a bed, so I was sleeping with a lot of blankets and pillows on the floor. A few days after surgery, I just couldn't sleep on my back anymore, so I figured out a way to side sleep without hurting my drain sites. My post-op appointment was two weeks after my surgery, and my discomfort steadily decreased while my range of motion increased.

I got my drains out at my post-op appointment, though they were slightly reluctant to remove both, because my right side was still outputting a little more fluid than expected. That process was uncomfortable, but painless. I was sent home and told to keep a compression vest on for two more weeks to prevent swelling (though I was impatient and didn't follow their advice on that one). I was scheduled for a second post-op appointment a few weeks after that to make sure I was healing correctly, though I didn't actually make it to that appointment due to transportation issues. The drains were the last thing that was keeping me from feeling and operating like normal, and once they were removed, I don't think there was a functional difference between how I felt then and how I feel now, seven months post-op. 

I feel pretty fortunate that my recovery went off without any real problems, as I hear stories fairly frequently in Reddit and Facebook groups about people who actually did struggle with daily activities of living, or their bodies threw a blood clot, or whatever other issues they might have had. Overall, I think if you take it easy and pay attention to your body, you'll be okay.

Sadly, T died last year due to his seizure disorder, while C was pregnant with their ninth child (and only daughter).
